processing: The flower heads are dried whole. No further processing steps are well documented.
harvest_season: Picked when the plant flowers; little is documented on picking dates.
appearance_dry: Small dried flower heads, dark with a reddish-brown tone.
appearance_liquor: A deep blood red, the reason locals also call it blood chrysanthemum.
appearance_wet: Soft small flower heads that give up their colour and darken the water.
taste_profile: Few reliable tasting notes exist; as with other flower-head infusions, expect a floral, herbal cup. The colour is the striking part.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for dried flowers, not a documented traditional method. A glass cup shows off the colour.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage. As usual for dried flowers, buy the latest harvest and drink it within a year or so. Wild Kunlun origin is the selling point, but the plant is widely cultivated and naturalised in China, so much of the market need not be wild.
description:
Despite the name, this is not a true chrysanthemum. Xue ju is the dried flower head of Coreopsis tinctoria, plains coreopsis, a North American annual in the daisy family that also grows in China. The Kunlun name refers to wild plants in the high mountains of Xinjiang.

The one thing that sets it apart is colour. A small pinch of heads turns water deep red, which earned it the local nickname blood chrysanthemum.

Flavour is less well recorded than colour, so go by your own cup. Use hot water and a modest amount, as you would with other dried flowers, and steep for a few minutes in glass.

When buying, keep the botany in mind: real chrysanthemum teas like hangbaiju are a different plant and a pale cup. Kunlun on a label is hard to verify, since cultivated plants are common, and health claims from sellers are just that.
history:
Little is documented about how long the flower has been drunk in Xinjiang. Writing on it is recent and comes mainly from chemistry and food science.

The species itself is native to North America and is now widely grown and naturalised in China, so the Kunlun identity rests on place and on wild growth in the mountains, not on a plant unique to them.
